title: The convergence of hematology and immunology (November 13–15; Tianjin, China)
abstract: The Convergence of Hematology and Immunology (CHI), which was sponsored by State Key Laboratory of Experimental Hematology, Institute of Hematology and Blood Diseases Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (CAMS), was held in Tianjin, China. Co-chaired by Tao Cheng of Institute of Hematology and Blood Diseases Hospital at CAMS (Tianjin, China), Lai Guan NG, and Florent Ginhoux of Singapore Immunology Network (Singapore), the two-day meeting invited 34 scientists from China, the United States, Singapore, Israel, Sweden, Switzerland, Japan, Italy, and Australia to present and share their latest views on the topics in hematology and immunology. This meeting has attracted more than 300 scientists and students. The highlights of the Convergence of Hematology and Immunology include keynote lectures, invited talks, and lighting talks selected from submitted abstracts. Another major milestone of this meeting was the announcement of the official opening of the Belt and Road Joint Laboratory. It would be impossible to highlight all the excellent speeches in this short report, but we hope to provide a glimpse of the topics discussed in the meeting. Prof. Sten Eirik Jacobsen of Karolinska Institute gave the first keynote speech focusing on the heterogeneity and lineage restriction within the hematopoietic stem cell compartment. After introducing previous single-cell transplantation studies, which uncovered considerable heterogeneity in lineage bias and restriction among reconstituting hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), he suggested that such lineage bias or restriction might reflect generation of lineage-restricted unipotent or oligopotent self-renewing progenitors within the phenotypic HSC compartment. He next showed their published work, which uncovered a highly organized, predictable, and stable framework for lineage-restricted fates of long-term self-renewing HSCs following transplantation into myeloablated recipients. Single HSC transplantation and serial assessment of all blood lineages revealed limited and hierarchically related repertoire of adult LT-HSCs undergoing lineage-restricted fates. He emphasized that they identified the only single-lineage-restricted adult mouse HSCs (platelet-restricted), which adopted a fate toward effective and stable replenishment of a megakaryocyte/platelet lineage tree but not any other blood cell lineages, despite their sustained multipotency. Long-term genetic lineage tracing supports an important role of platelet-biased HSCs in unperturbed adult hematopoiesis. Platelet-biased HSCs expand upon aging. Until now, they found no evidence for lymphoid-biased LT-HSCs. Their work uncovers a limited repertoire of distinct HSC subsets, defined by a predictable and hierarchical propensity to adopt a fate toward replenishment of a restricted set of blood cell lineages following transplantation, before loss of self-renewal and multipotency. Prof. Paul Frenette of Albert Einstein College of Medicine gave the second keynote speech reviewing the work on hematopoietic microenvironment and aging of HSCs, as well as highlighting a novel “don’t eat me” pathway regulating acute myeloid leukemia clearance by phagocytes. It is well accepted that HSCs suffer a decline in their regenerative capacity and multi-lineage differentiation potential, leading to impaired immune responses and the development of hematologic malignancies. He showed that arterioles and megakaryocytes conferred specific microenvironments regulating functionally distinct subset of HSCs. Aging is associated with significant reductions in innervating adrenergic nerve fibers in the bone marrow. Denervation of the bone marrow of young mice produces all the hallmarks of HSC aging, including myeloid bias with lymphopenia and diminished repopulation capacity. Supplementation of a β3-adrenoreceptor agonist to old mice significantly rejuvenated the in vivo function of aged HSCs by acting on bone marrow stromal cells. Vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (Vcam1) is an adhesion molecule expressed on macrophages, endothelial cells, and stromal cells. It mediates homing and retention of HSCs and progenitors into bone marrow. The recent studies by his group investigating the role of the macrophage niche in hematopoiesis revealed novel functions for Vcam1. They found that Vcam1 was also expressed on HSCs, and upregulated in human and mouse AML cases. High Vcam1 expression was associated with shorter survival. Further work demonstrated that Vcam1 played a role in the recognition of “self,” regulating AML progression via clearance inhibition by phagocytosis. Mononuclear phagocyte depletion prevented the clearance of Vcam1Δ/Δ AML cells. Hence, he suggested that targeting Vcam1 might represent a promising approach to eliminate leukemic stem cells in AML. Prof. Yasmine Belkaid of NIH gave the third keynote speech on the two interesting topics. First, how immune system adapts to transient nutritional stress. She showed that dietary restriction redirected memory T cells from secondary lymphoid organs to the bone marrow. This response is also accompanied by profound bone marrow compartment remodeling, erythropoiesis and adipogenesis. Prof. Belkaid also provided evidence to illustrate that enhanced T cell accumulation in the bone marrow was to preserve immunological memory during dietary stress. The other topic discussed was about how the host microbiota influenced immune responses. Specifically, she discussed about how microbiota affected the training of mucosal-associated invariant T cells (MAIT cells) at the early life exposure and would have a long-term impact on the development of immune response (protective during infection). This imprinting of MAIT cells is time sensitive, after this period MAIT cell development will be permanently impaired. Prof. Ido Amit of Weizmann Institute of Science gave the fourth keynote speech entitled “The power of ONE: immunology in the age of single cell genomics.” He highlighted single-cell genomics, which hold the potential to revolutionize the way we characterize complex immune cell assemblies through the study of their spatial organization, dynamics, clonal distribution, pathways, and crosstalk. He provided an overview of how recent single-cell genomic studies are changing the perspective of various immune-related pathologies from cancer to neurodegeneration. Following this, he introduced a technology called physical interacting cell sequencing, which would be a powerful tool to study interaction between two kinds of immune cells. First, the doublets, which contained two kinds of physically contacted immune cells, were sorted by FACS. Then the specific type of cells was separated from the doublets and sorted by FACS before they underwent single-cell sequencing. By using this technology, his group studied interactions between T cells and dendritic cells (DCs), showing that Tregs have high capacity to interact with DCs. Additionally, he also provided an overview of another novel technology called posttranslational modification sequencing, which coupled intracellular protein staining and single-cell sequencing technique. How this technique works is based on fixation, permeabilization, and RNA preservation of cells, followed by labeling with antibody against intracellular proteins and single-cell sequencing. Prof. Amit provided some of their preliminary data that revealed that MDSCs possessed unique signaling/metabolism activities such as ROS, iNOS, and ARG1. Prof. Chen Dong of Tsinghua University presented the works from his laboratory. He first showed from their genome-wide analysis, his group identified transcription factor NR4A1 was a key regulator for T cell activation. Their data showed that overexpression of NR4A1 inhibited T cell activation and differentiation and, on the contrary, deletion of NR4A1 broke T cell tolerance. Moreover, his group also identified transcription factor Tox2 that regulated differentiation of T follicular helper. Additionally, they also provided evidence to show that the Tox2-BCL6 axis formed the transcriptional network that was crucial for T follicular helper program. Prof. Jinyong Wang of Chinese Academy of Sciences brought the story about regeneration of transplantable T cell precursors from pluripotent stem cells by defined factors. His group established a new method to generate engraftable hematopoietic progenitors in vitro from pluripotent stem cells (iR9-PSC), which are capable of homing to thymus and developing into mature T (iT) cells in primary and secondary immunodeficient recipients. This differentiation is induced by synergistic and transient expression of Runx1 and Hoxa9 restricted in the time window of endothelial to hematopoietic transition and hematopoietic maturation stages. Notably, the iT cells distributed normally in central and peripheral lymphoid organs and exhibited abundant TCRαβ repertoire. The regenerative T lymphopoiesis rescued the immune surveillance ability in immunodeficient mice. Prof. Wang also presented data to show that gene-edited iR9-PSC produced tumor-specific-T cells in vivo that can effectively eradicate tumor cells. Collectively, their work provides insight into universal generation of functional and therapeutic T lymphopoiesis from the unlimited and editable PSC source. HSC transplantation is widely used in treatment of hematopoietic and nonhematopoietic disorders. However, how transplanted HSCs reconstitute hematopoiesis at the early stage after transplantation has not been elucidated due to technical limitations. Prof. Tao Cheng of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences gave a speech on rapid differentiation of transplanted hematopoietic stem cells revealed by single-cell transcriptomics. Based on single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, his group identified 28 transcriptionally distinct subpopulations of hematopoietic cells. To understand the dynamic changes of transplanted HSCs in irradiated recipients, they tracked these cells within the first week after transplantation. Unexpectedly, the majority of the transplanted HSCs rapidly differentiated into multipotent progenitors. Occasionally, the HSCs gave rise to megakaryocytic/erythroid or myeloid precursors via a noncanonical differentiation path. Further work demonstrated that the cells arrived in the bone marrow from day 1 to day 7 progressively decreased the long-term reconstitution capability. This work uncovered the kinetics and fate choices of transplanted HSCs in myeloablated recipients at early stage and may have implications for clinical applications of HSCs and other stem cells. Macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells play crucial and distinct roles in tissue homeostasis and immunity. They also contribute to a broad spectrum of pathologies and are attractive therapeutic targets. Dr. Florent Ginhoux of Singapore Immunology Network reviewed their major work on dendritic cell and macrophage biology: from development to functions, providing deep insights of the origins and the mechanisms that govern their homeostasis and activation. In his talk, he first discussed about the origin of macrophages. He provided an overview of various data to show that macrophages arise from successive waves of embryonic and adult hematopoiesis, and that tissue resident macrophages in most tissues are established prenatally and self-maintained throughout adulthood. In adults, the origin of macrophages is heterogeneous. Monocyte-derived macrophages contribute to resident macrophages during adulthood but the kinetics and the degree of contribution varies among tissues. Subsequently, he discussed the heterogeneity of lung interstitial macrophages. By single-cell sequencing and transcriptomic analysis, two subpopulations, MHCII+ and MHCII− macrophages, were identified in lung interstitial macrophages. Further work demonstrated that the macrophage dichotomy was conserved across tissues. Moreover, two distinct interstitial macrophage subpopulations coexist across tissues in unique subcellular niches. He next showed that the Lyve1+ macrophages inhibited recruitment of inflammatory cells and fibrosis. During inflammation, adult-derived and embryonic-derived macrophages had different dynamics, that is, tissue-resident macrophages proliferate upon mild injury; both tissue-resident macrophages and monocyte-derived macrophages proliferate upon HSV skin infection and atherosclerosis; monocyte-derived macrophages proliferate upon severe inflammatory injuries. In the last part of his talk, he discussed about a molecule, Ms4a3, which was highly and specifically expressed in GMPs, GPs, and cMoPs but not in tissue-resident macrophage or DCs. Based on this information, they established several Ms4a3-based reporter mouse models, including Ms4a3TdT reporter, Ms4a3Cre-RosaTdT, and Ms4a3CreERT2-RosaTdT mouse models. Using these models, his group precisely quantified the contribution of monocytes to the tissue-resident macrophage pool during homeostasis and inflammation. The group of Prof. Bertie Göttgens of University of Cambridge has long been interested in deciphering the regulatory networks that control the development of blood cells in the embryo, homeostasis of the blood system in the adult, and how specific mutations can initiate system perturbations that ultimately lead to malignant transformation. In this meeting, he pointed out that cell atlas projects are important but descriptive. We need to find ways to address the mechanism leading to cellular decision-making in hematopoietic system. His group is undergoing multidisciplinary work combining single-cell molecular profiling, bioinformatics analysis, and experimental/functional validation to study the processes. He first reviewed advances in early organogenesis at single-cell resolution, such as scRNA-Seq atlas of mouse development from E6.5 to E8.5, new pipeline to access key regulatory genes by Chimera-Seq, defined molecular defect in cellular decision-making in Tal1−/−, new pathway involved in blood development, and validated Notch1 in Endo/Myocardium diversification. He then turned to their work in cellular decision-making in hematopoietic cells. By using a library containing 38 single-guided RNAs of transcription factors, his group screened 19 transcription factors important for lineage determination. These factors have many targets and formed complex interaction network, and they focused on two transcription factors, Ebf1 and Gata3, which are important for T/B lineage determination in progenitors. Prof. Timm Schroeder of ETH Zurich gave a talk entitled “Long-term single-cell quantification: new tools for old questions.” He pointed out the limitation of cell research, that is, we usually analyzed populations of cells rather than individual cells, and we take a “snapshot” view on a dynamic process. The immune system is a complex, dynamic, and plastic network composed of various interacting cell types that are constantly sensing and responding to environmental cues. Hence, his group developed imaging systems and software to image, segment, and track cells long term and to quantify divisional history, position, interaction, and protein expression or activity of all individual cells over many generations. These datasets were used for analyzing the dynamics, interplay, and functions of signaling pathway and transcription factor networks in controlling hematopoietic, pluripotent, skeletal, and neural stem cell fate decisions. HSCs are responsible for the life-long maintenance of blood production. In aging individuals, HSCs lose their regenerative capacity and show typical features of blood aging, including immunosenescence, anemia, and skewed myeloid cell production. The bone marrow HSC niche contributes in these processes. By using FACS, single-cell sequencing, and immunofluorescence, Prof. Emmanuelle Passegue of Columbia University discussed about the remodeling of the entire bone marrow niche microenvironment during aging process, such as remodeling of stromal compartment with the loss of endothelial compartment. In later part of her talk, Prof. Passegue touched on the role of cytokines in HSCs and progenitors. In particular, she mentioned TNFα and IL-1 signaling pathways in promoting aging in HSCs, which led to accumulation of poorly regenerative myeloid-biased old HSCs. After that, they provided evidence to show inhibition of IL-1 pathway with IL-1 antagonist in old mice in an improvement of old HSC regeneration upon 5-FU challenge. Lifestyle factors are well known to contribute to cardiovascular disease. Prof. Filip Swirski of Harvard University gave a talk on systemic inflammatory networks in cardiovascular disease. He focused on how lifestyle factors such as diet and sleep may impact on hematopoiesis and atherosclerosis. He presented how sleep can modulate CSF-1 production by pre-neutrophils to modulate monocyte production and atherosclerosis. Thus, this talk highlighted the importance of neuroimmune axis in modulation of hematopoiesis and disease outcome. Finally, the meeting ends with the final talk from Dr. Shachi Bhatt, the scientific editor of Journal of Experimental Medicine. She introduced the scope of the journal and the reviewing process of the journal, such as how the journal selects their referees, what the journal expects from the referees, how the editors make the decision based on referee's comments. This talk is especially useful for junior staff as it provides insights into the manuscript submission and review process of a top-tier journal. We also apologize to the many great speakers who attended this meeting but whose talks could not be discussed in this meeting report. These include Burkhard Becher of University of Zurich, Lee Grimes of Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, Bo Zhou of Shanghai Institute of Biochemistry and Cell Biology, Emery Bresnick of University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health, Jia Yu of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Lai Guan Ng of Singapore Immunology Network, Jing Wang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Chong Shu Zhen of Singapore Immunology Network, Scott Mueller of the University of Melbourne, Junke Zheng of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Matteo Iannacone of San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Hongbo Hu of Sichuan University, Ashley St. John of Duke-NUS, Hongbo Luo of Harvard University, Veronique Angeli of National University of Singapore, Naomi McGovern of University of Cambridge, Simon Yona of Hebrew University, Bing Su of Shanghai Institute of Immunology, Pengxu Qian of Zhejiang University, Satoshi Yamazaki of University of Tokyo, and Daniel Saban of Duke University who presented their work in hematology and immunology. The inaugural convergence of hematology and immunology meeting was a great success. Hematology and immunology are closely related research field. This was the first meeting allowing hematologists and immunologists around the world to discuss fundamental hematologic and immunologic questions and to share advances in both areas, which would help researchers in both areas to gain spark of thought leading to new ideas. The meeting also provided a chance for young scientists and graduate students in China to know advances in the field of both hematology and immunology from high-quality speeches, which would help them to gain deeper understanding of the two areas and have beneficial impact on their future career pathways.

title: All is balanced: inter‐ α ‐trypsin inhibitors as unseen extracellular matrix proteins in epidermal morphology and differentiation
abstract: A growing number of epidermal diseases have been attributed to defects in epidermal structure, such as the cytoskeleton or cellular junctions, in terminal keratinocyte differentiation and the well-levelled linkage and detachment of corneocytes, and in signalling pathways for instance leading to altered proliferative properties of keratinocytes 1, 2. Many of these processes rely on the readiness of proteases. Given their vast importance in organ development and maintenance, their activity has to be controlled on different levels, not only must they be available in the right moment of cellular differentiation, but also have to be instantly switchable. A large number of different proteases are therefore synthesized in different layers of the skin, and they are closely controlled by a collection of protease inhibitors. The importance of protease cascades is illustrated by the fact that several skin diseases can be caused by mutations in a single protease or protease inhibitor 3, which would lead to disturbed cornification and eventually a defective epidermal barrier function. Recent developments in genetics and genomics have resulted in the identification of numerous mutations that cause monogenic skin diseases; however, our knowledge about the molecular pathogenesis of these diseases and especially multifactorial skin diseases is still rather limited. New generations of sequencing technologies have facilitated high-throughput approaches to study DNA sequences and gene expression with growing depth and speed. The understanding of global gene expression profiles, however, is still hindered by both technical and biological limitations. The analysis of the transcriptome has become possible, at least for single cell types and tissues, using microarray-based methods, and these approaches have already resulted in an accumulation of large amounts of valuable data. In contrast, the analysis of certain developmental (or pathological) processes and the comparison of large numbers of samples are quite arduous and thus restricted with these methods. The use of high-throughput sequencing for transcriptome analysis with RNA-seq has made these studies possible 4, 5. On the other hand, disadvantages of either method have been widely discussed; while the detection rates for various transcripts are much bigger with RNA-seq, limitations in the discovery of differential expression of poorly expressed genes have to be taken into account 6. Expression analyses of single genes or gene families using high-throughput approaches thus allow thorough studies of cell-type or disease-specific gene expression patterns and open new possibilities for the characterization of pathologies and mechanisms involved in the development of multifactorial disorders. One such gene family, which has been only poorly characterized so far and mostly in the context of tumor development, is the family of inter-α-trypsin inhibitors (ITIs), a group of plasma serine protease inhibitors. ITIs consist of a light chain, also referred to as bikunin (OMIM 176870), and a number of various heavy chains (ITIH1–ITIH6). ITI heavy chains are supposed to play a role in extracellular matrix stabilization through their binding to hyaluronic acid 7. Bikunin and ITI heavy chains have been proposed to be involved in carcinogenesis and metastasis, and they can contribute to inflammation as acute-phase proteins in various conditions. Few data are available on their differential expression during carcinogenesis, pointing to the loss of ITI heavy chains in human solid tumors 8. Current RNA-seq approaches have embarked on a systematic collection of gene expression data from various human tissues, which are particularly useful to characterize members of gene families and propose differential functions and activities in as yet disregarded tissues. Data made available in the Expression Atlas 9 illustrate the prospects of these experiments. An overview of RNA-seq results (Illumina Human Body Map; 10) regarding the ITI heavy chain genes ITIH1–ITIH5 (Fig. 1) demonstrates that ITIH1–ITIH4 are predominantly expressed in liver and ITIH5 though is mainly expressed in breast, adipose tissue and placenta. A recent study published in Experimental Dermatology 11 has now investigated the importance of ITIH5 (OMIM 609783) in skin, where it is moderately expressed, in contrast to the absent expression of ITIH1–ITIH4 (Fig. 1). Based on the finding of gene expression obtained with a targeted microarray-based approach in liver and skin, the authors have demonstrated that ITIH5 is found in normal dermal fibroblasts, but not in epidermal keratinocytes. Interestingly, they found an upregulation in inflammatory skin diseases, namely psoriasis, atopic dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis. ITIH5 was identified in these conditions in suprabasal layers of the epidermis, in particular in the respective areas of immune reactions. The importance of ITIs for inflammatory disorders is further suggested by their accumulation in lichen sclerosus in the upper dermal areas where hyaluronan is abnormally deposited 12. The study of epidermal ITIs sheds light on the role of hyaluronan for epidermal structure and function. Itih5 knockout mice and ITIH5-deficient murine epidermal equivalents showed thinning of the epidermis, reduced proliferative capacities and disturbed epidermal cornification 11. On the other hand, application of exogenous hyaluronan to skin equivalents resulted in increased proliferation and enhanced development of the epidermal lipid barrier 13. Hyaluronan signalling is mediated through CD44 binding and supposed to be enhanced by ITI heavy chains and other hyaluronan-associated proteins 7. It is essential for proper keratinocyte differentiation, where it is potentially implemented by the elevation of intracellular Ca2+ levels 14. Regulatory pathways in the skin involving ITIH5 have not been explored so far, but they might give exciting new insight into basic cutaneous mechanisms including wound healing and skin ageing. The finding of ITIH5 in the skin underlines the importance of global gene expression studies for the understanding of tissue function and disease. Functional studies of signalling pathways and protein networks are now required, and advanced model systems, necessarily also models representing human tissues and human cells, are on the way for systematic analyses in a larger scale. Unrecognized regulatory molecules, however, can give decisive clues to mechanisms of epidermal homeostasis. The author has no conflict of interest to declare.

title: Refining Radiation for the Next Century
abstract: Wilhelm Röentgen's report more than a century ago describing X-ray imaging fostered in the application of ionizing radiation (IR) for cancer therapy. Today, about half of all the patients with cancer are treated with radiotherapy and it remains one of our most effective treatment modalities, much to the surprise of many of my Cancer Biology friends. The use of altered fractionation schedules and image-guided radiotherapy has significantly improved patient outcomes. The concomitant administration of radiation with chemotherapy or targeted agents has been shown to sensitize malignant cells or in some cases protect nonmalignant cells. We now know that the stress and damage caused by IR to nonmalignant and malignant cells evokes adaptive changes that can also be targeted for treatment strategies. Nonetheless, many patients with cancer fail to benefit from these advances in IR treatment protocols and, therefore, efforts to refine further the potential of radiotherapy continue.Induction of DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) is one of the fundamental mechanisms by which IR kills tumor cells. Cells, however, have evolved elaborate lesion recognition, signal transmission, cell-cycle synchronization, and damage restoration networks that reduce the potential lethal effects of IR and other stresses. In eukaryotic cells, there are two major mechanisms of DSB repair: homologous recombination and nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ). NHEJ operates throughout the cell cycle, works in a template-independent manner, and repairs as much as 85% of IR-induced DSBs in the mammalian cells.Our emerging understanding of the prosurvival pathways that malignant cells maintain and the mechanisms by which nonmalignant and malignant cells respond to IR damage have stimulated thoughtful searches for new molecular therapeutic strategies that would enhance IR. In this issue of Molecular Cancer Therapeutics, there are nine illustrations of how our emerging knowledgebase is being exploited to advance the use of IR for the treatment of glioblastoma, non–small cell lung cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and prostate cancer. Collectively, these articles highlight the frontiers of modern molecular cancer radiotherapy and are likely to help ensure that IR remains a central pillar for cancer therapy in this century.Several articles in this issue focus on enhancing the efficacy of IR toward glioblastoma, which remains a poorly responsive lethal disease. The TCGA database reveals that >80% of all glioblastoma have genetic alterations in the PI3K and p53 pathways, which are heavily involved in genotoxic stress and cell fate decisions. Alterations in the PI3K pathway cause the constitutive activation of AKT, which is both progrowth and prosurvival. Conversely, p53 activity is suppressed in most glioblastomas, predominantly from inactivating mutations or increased activity of the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase MDM2. Suppression of p53 activity alters DNA damage repair, apoptosis, and genetic stability. Palanichamy and colleagues (1) used a phosphatidylinositol ether lipid analogue (PIA), which blocks AKT activity by binding to the PIP3 site, to define the role of AKT and p53 in glioblastoma. They observed the p53-mt, but not the p53 wild-type glioblastoma cell lines, were sensitized to IR when pretreated with PIA two hours prior to radiation exposure in culture. The radiation sensitization corresponded with an increase in DNA damage and a decrease in the levels of DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunits (DNA-PKcs), which are involved in the fast component of the radiation-induced DNA DSB repair pathway involving NHEJ. Radiation sensitization was not observed in normal human astrocytes. The authors concluded that the increased DNA damage in glioblastoma cell lines with functionally mutant or null p53 results from the downregulation of DNA-PKcs and propose inhibition of AKT might be a therapeutic strategy for TP53-mutant glioblastomas (1). It should be noted, however, that the glioblastoma cells used in the study had hundreds of mutations in TP53, which raises the question of whether the type of p53 mutation matters for the synthetic lethality. It is also unclear how selective an AKT inhibitor needs to be, as the allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 produced sensitization to IR in glioblastoma cells that was independent of the p53 status. IR sensitization of glioblastoma was also observed with an inhibitor of the MAPK pathway, MEK162 or binimetinib, which downregulated and dephosphorylated the cell-cycle checkpoint proteins CDK1/CDK2/WEE1 and DNA damage response proteins phosphorylated ATM or CHK2 (2). When combined with IR, the MEK1/2 inhibitor binimetinib prolonged DNA damage and increased apoptosis probably by abrogating the G2–M checkpoint. When binimetinib was combined with IR treatment in an orthotopic glioblastoma model, synergistic tumor growth reduction was seen with the combination treatment and a significantly longer median survival time compared with vehicle control.The PI3K and AKT pathways are also activated by the tyrosine kinase receptors MET, AXL, and FGFR. All three receptors have been associated with mechanisms of resistance to conventional and targeted therapies. S49076 is an oral ATP-competitive inhibitor of MET, AXL, and FGFR1–3 receptors that is currently in phase I/II clinical trials. As with many tyrosine kinase inhibitors, other molecular targets can emerge with more detailed studies and the examination of higher drug concentrations. Clémenson and colleagues (3) found that S49076 at low concentrations, as predicted, caused MET-dependent cytotoxicity through MET inhibition but at higher (but still clinically relevant) concentrations inhibited the growth of MET-independent cells by targeting Aurora B. S49076 improved the antitumor efficacy of IR in both MET-dependent and MET-independent cell lines in vitro and in subcutaneous and orthotopic tumor models in vivo. Thus, future studies may wish to evaluate S49076 with IR in clinical trials without patient selection based on the tumor MET dependency status.Radiotherapy, like others forms of stress, is known to activate prosurvival pathways, such as AKT and mTORC, which limit the efficacy of systemic treatments including cytotoxic and targeted therapies. Eke and colleagues (4) explored this adaptive response and found IR increased the AKT and mTOR phosphorylation and the constellation of protein with which they interact in 3D prostate cancer models and tumor xenografts. They documented that pharmacologic inhibitors of AKT (GDC-0068) and mTOR signaling (INK128) were more effective against prostate cancer cells when given after multifractionated IR treatment compared with before IR. These studies are an important proof-of-principle because they highlight the dynamic nature of the survival pathways in tumors after IR exposure. Simply looking at the genomic composition of the tumor prior to treatment without taking into account that the efficiency of targeted drugs can also be modulated by stress-induced protein modifications may be misleading. It may be possible to use IR to prime tumors for enhanced drug-induced killing. It remains unanswered, however, whether this concept will be useful in vivo for disseminated tumors or just for local prostate cancer.Protein proteolysis occurs via the 26S proteasome using E3 ligases and substrate recognition subunits, which confer specificity for the targeted polyubiquitylated substrates. Cullin RING E3 ubiquitin Ligase 4 (CRL4) with the substrate recognition subunit CDT2 is a master regulator of genome stability and the cell cycle, primarily through the targeted proteolysis of the replication licensing protein CDT1, the CDK inhibitor p21, and the histone methyltransferase SET8 during S-phase of the cell cycle. CDT2 is activated, and its substrates are degraded, following IR-induced DNA damage and this is important for DNA repair and IR-induced early G2–M checkpoint. CDT2-mediated ubiquitylation of CDT1, SET8 and p21 in S-phase of unperturbed cells prevents reinitiation of DNA replication, a phenomenon termed DNA rereplication. Rereplication is deleterious to cells and, in some cases, induces cellular senescence or apoptosis due to the accumulation of toxic replication intermediates and replication fork stalling. Previous studies found that the neddylation inhibitor pevonedistat or MLN4924 inhibits cancer cell lines and tumors and is associated with significant induction of DNA rereplication. Vanderdys and colleagues (5) demonstrated that induction of rereplication genetically or pharmacologically induced robust IR sensitization in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells and tumors. Specifically, they found treating mice with penvonedistat 2 hours prior to IR caused significantly greater suppression of the growth of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma xenografts compared with either modality alone. They suggest that pevonedistat may be a possible adjuvant for IR-based treatments.Groselj and colleagues (6) employed an innovative in vivo technique to evaluate the IR sensitization by the pan-histone deacetylase inhibitor panobinostat using subcutaneous xenografts in athymic nude mice. Panobinostat did not add to the acute intestinal toxicity caused by 10–14 Gy IR nor did it increase the delayed IR intestinal and bladder toxicity. The combination of panobinostat with IR was superior to IR alone in reducing bladder cancer xenograft growth but overall survival was not measured. IR sensitization by panobinostat was associated with class I histone deacetylase inhibition and protein downregulation of HDAC2 and MRE11.It has been known for decades that tumor cells are highly sensitive to arginine deficiency. A proof-of-principle in vitro arginine deprivation therapy study was performed using recombinant human arginase or arginine-free diets. Significant IR sensitization was detected and it was more pronounced in 2D and 3D glioblastoma cell models with cells lacking functional p53 compared with their p53-wild-type counterparts (7). Further work will be needed to define the underlying mechanism responsible for this sensitization and whether or not it can be seen in preclinical mouse models.The popularity of synthetic lethal strategies has stimulated several groups to seek new IR sensitizers using high-throughput screening methods focused on DNA repair. In some cases, investigators have explored drug repurposing as a faster, more efficient, and economical route for new IR sensitizers. One example is the lipophilic statin, pitavastatin, which was identified as a potent inhibitor of DSB repair in breast and melanoma models both in vitro and in vivo (8). When combined with IR, pitavastatin increased persistent DSBs, induced senescence, and enhanced acute effects of IR on IR-resistant melanoma tumors. shRNA knockdown studies implicated inhibition of protein prenylation rather than cholesterol biosynthesis for the sensitization. The authors conclude that we should consider repurposing pitavastatin or other lipophilic statins as possible IR sensitizers.Another innovative screening approach looked for NHEJ inhibitors by using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) system and high-resolution melting analysis (9). The assay relied on the error-prone nature of the NHEJ-mediated ligation of the site-specific DSB induced by Cas9 nuclease to cause the mutation of the targeted sequence as detected by high-resolution melting analysis. Armed with this assay, the authors probed a 1,540-compound drug library and identified the cardiac glycoside ouabain and the first-generation antipsychotic penfluridol inhibited NHEJ activity and sensitized HeLa cells to IR. Ouabin and penfluridol have a number of other pharmacologic effects and have not been evaluated with IR in vivo so further screening and optimization are likely to be required. Nonetheless, this is an interesting cell-based screening platform for NHEJ inhibitors, which could assist in the discovery of novel sensitizers of IR.Both the bone marrow and the gastrointestinal tract are highly sensitivity to IR toxicity. Morita and colleagues (10) found that 5-chloro-8-quinolinol (5CHQ), albeit at high concentrations, shifted p53 transactivation activity from proapoptotic to antiapoptotic by enhancing p21 induction and suppressing PUMA induction. This p53-modulating effect seemed to be attributable to the sequence-specific alteration of p53 DNA-binding, as evaluated by chromatin immunoprecipitation and electrophoretic mobility shift assays. The authors found 5CHQ protected the hematopoietic and gastrointestinal system in mouse irradiation models with dose reduction factors in total body and abdominally irradiated mice of about 1.2 and 1.3, respectively. 5CHQ effectively protected mouse epithelial stem cells from a lethal dose of abdominal irradiation. These results provide initial evidence that the pharmacologic upregulation of IR-protective p53-target genes as a potential strategy for addressing the gastrointestinal syndrome.Radiotherapy continues to evolve. The articles in this issue demonstrate the multidisciplinary muscle that is required for therapeutic advancement and the value of combining the unique skills found in the field of Radiation Biology, namely quantitative analytics of DNA damage and repair, biophysics, and replication death measurements, with those of other fields, such as signal transduction, bioinformatics, gene expression, genomics, proteomics and pharmacology. There is fertile soil for the growth of new IR strategies for cancer treatments even after a century of the discovery of X-rays.See all articles in this MCT Focus section, “Developmental Therapeutics in Radiation Oncology.”The author is grateful for continuous support from the NIH, the Department of Defense, the Fiske Drug Discovery Fund, and the Owen Family Foundation.

title: Insertional mutagenesis in the vascular wilt pathogen Verticillium dahliae
abstract: Vascular wilt diseases caused by soil-borne pathogens are among the most devastating plant diseases worldwide. The ascomycete fungus Verticillium dahliae causes vascular wilt diseases in hundreds of dicotyledonous plant species, including important crops such as eggplant, lettuce, olive, spinach and tomato. The resting structures, microsclerotia, are triggered by root exudates to germinate and penetrate the roots after which the fungus grows into the xylem vessels. The fungus colonizes these vessels and interferes with the transportation of water and nutrients, resulting in the development of symptoms such as stunting, wilting, chlorosis and vascular browning. Verticillium wilt diseases are difficult to control due to the longevity of the microsclerotia, the broad host range of the pathogen, the inability of fungicides to kill the fungus once it has colonized the xylem vessels and the lack of natural resistance in many plant species. Chapter 1 is the introduction to this thesis that describes the identified pathogenicity and virulence factors of V. dahliae and strategies to identify these components. In spite of the economic importance of V. dahliae, relatively few pathogenicity genes have been identified in this species. With the availability of whole genome sequences and the development of functional genomics tools such as random mutagenesis, targeted mutagenesis, transcriptomics, RNA interference (RNAi) and comparative genomics, more strategies have become available to identify novel pathogenicity and virulence genes. Chapter 2 focuses on the identification of virulence and pathogenicity genes of V. dahliae by screening of a library of random T-DNA insertion mutants. Using Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation, 900 T-DNA transformants with random insertions were generated and screened for altered virulence on susceptible tomato plants. This screening, followed by inverse PCR on selected transformants, resulted in the identification of 55 potential pathogenicity and virulence genes. One of the potential pathogenicity genes, VdNRS/ER, is a homolog of a nucleotide-rhamnose synthase/epimerase-reductase (NRS/ER), which is presumably involved in the biosynthesis of UDP-rhamnose. Using targeted mutagenesis, VdNRS/ER was deleted from wild-type V. dahliae and the resulting deletion mutants were characterized. VdNRS/ER deletion mutants exhibit unaltered vegetative growth and sporulation, but the deletion mutants were no longer pathogenic on tomato and N. benthamiana and showed impaired root attachment on tomato seedlings. These data suggest that UDPrhamnose is required for pathogenesis of V. dahliae. Chapter 3 describes the role of the V. dahliae homolog of Sge1, a transcriptional regulator that was shown to play a role in pathogenicity and regulate effector gene expression in Fusarium oxysporum. In this chapter it is demonstrated that V. dahliae Sge1 (VdSge1) is required for radial growth and production of asexual conidiospores. It is furthermore shown that VdSge1 deletion strains have lost pathogenicity on tomato. Since the VdSge1 deletion mutants are not able to infect and colonize tomato plants, a tomato cell suspension culture was used to the study the expression of Ave1, as well as nine other genes of which the expression is highly induced in planta. This assay revealed that VdSge1 is not required for the induction of the Ave1 effector that activates resistance mediated by Ve1 in tomato. Furthermore, the expression of one other putative effector gene was not affected by VdSge1 deletion. However, VdSge1 was shown to be required for the expression of six putative effector genes, whereas expression of the remaining two putative effectors genes was negatively regulated. Thus, the data show that VdSge1 is required for V. dahliae pathogenicity and differentially regulates effector gene expression. Chapter 4 describes the functional characterization of the gene family encoding necrosis- and ethylene-inducing-like proteins (NLPs) of V. dahliae. The cytotoxic activity of NLP family members was determined using agroinfiltration into tobacco leaves. This resulted in the identification of two out of the seven NLPs, VdNLP1 and VdNLP2, that induced plant cell death. The genes encoding these cytotoxic NLPs were found to be induced in V. dahliae upon colonization of tomato. Targeted deletion of VdNLP1 and VdNLP2 significantly reduced the virulence of V. dahliae on tomato and Arabidopsis plants. In contrast, only deletion of VdNLP1 affected virulence on N. benthamiana whereas deletion of NLP2 did not. However, subsequent transcriptional analysis revealed that VdNLP2 was not expressed in V. dahliae during colonization of N. benthamiana. Moreover, VdNLP2 also affects vegetative growth and conidiospore production. In conclusion, the expanded V. dahliae NLP family shows differential cytotoxic activity between family members and in planta induction of the cytotoxic NLP genes varies between plant hosts. In addition, VdNLP2 plays a role in vegetative growth and conidiospore production in addition to its contribution to virulence. Thus, evidence is provided for functional diversification within the V. dahliae NLP family. Finally in Chapter 5, the major findings of this thesis are discussed and placed in a broader perspective.

title: Myelin lipid deficiency: a new key driver of Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Lipids play essential biological functions that include acting as components of biological membranes, energy storage, signaling, nutrients, transporters, enzyme activators, among others. Compared with the multiple research methods to assess DNA, RNA, and protein content, location, and function in cells, there are relatively fewer methods to study lipids. Therefore, lipid-oriented mechanistic studies remain rare and challenging. Lipidomics which allows large-scale analysis of cellular lipids, is a critical strategy for achieving this. One revolutionary advance in lipidomics pioneered by our group is the development of multidimensional mass spectrometry-based shotgun lipidomics, which has become a foundational analytical technology platform among current lipidomics practices due to its high efficiency, sensitivity, and reproducibility, as well as its broad coverage and minimal batch effects. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is by far the most common form of dementia. The number of people living with AD is growing up fast as the world population ages and life expectancy increases. Unfortunately, effective disease-modifying therapies remain elusive (Cummings et al., 2018), highlighting the importance of better understanding the molecular mechanism(s) underlying disease etiology. The brain is the richest organ in terms of lipid content and diversity, largely due to the abundance of lipid-rich myelin. On the other hand, large-scale human genome-wide association studies have consistently linked lipid metabolism with AD (Wightman et al., 2021). However, there are relatively few studies focusing on the mechanisms regarding how specific lipids, other than cholesterol, affect AD pathogenesis. By exploiting multidimensional mass spectrometry-based shotgun lipidomics, our laboratory has revealed that a class of myelin-enriched lipids, i.e., sulfatide, is dramatically reduced at the earliest clinically recognizable stages of AD and in AD animal models and specifically lost compared to other myelin lipids and other neuropathological conditions, which showed a strong relationship with ApoE4 (Han et al., 2003), the strongest genetic risk factor for AD. In a recent study (Qiu et al., 2021), we reported that mild central nervous system (CNS) myelin sulfatide losses are sufficient to activate disease-associated microglia and astrocytes, and to increase the expression of AD risk genes (e.g., Apoe, Trem2, Cd33, Mmp12, and Spi1), as well as previously established causal regulators of the immune/microglia network in late-onset AD (e.g., Tyrobp, Dock, and Fcerg1), leading to chronic AD-like neuroinflammation and mild cognitive impairment. Furthermore, CNS sulfatide deficiency-induced astrogliosis and astrocytic ApoE upregulation were independent of microgliosis. Notably, all the phenotypes showed gender differences, being more pronounced in females than males. To mimic and study the consequences and related molecular mechanisms of adult-onset sulfatide deficiency in very early AD, we generated a novel mouse model, i.e., myelinating cells specific cerebroside sulfotransferase (CST, a.k.a. Gal3st1) conditional knockout (cKO) mice. CST codes for the enzyme that catalyzes the last step of sulfatide biosynthesis. Myelin sulfatide is inducibly and conditionally depleted by tamoxifen in adult CST cKO mice. For the first time, multiple lines of evidence were provided at the lipid, RNA, and protein levels to demonstrate that inducible myelinating glia-specific CST depletion leads to specific losses of CNS sulfatide without major impact on overall oligodendrocyte/myelin homeostasis or cell death, but is sufficient to impair cognitive dysfunction, disrupting both spatial and non-spatial memory consolidation. Accumulating evidence has implicated sustained glia-mediated inflammation as a major contributor to AD neurodegenerative processes and cognitive deficits (Newcombe et al., 2018). In the study of the related cell/molecular mechanisms of adult-onset myelin sulfatide deficiency, we found that most upregulated gene expression after sulfatide loss was enriched in activated microglia and astrocytes, which overlapped with the AD disease-associated microglia and astrocytes, leading to chronic AD-like neuroinflammation. The predictions from transcription factors scores based on the significantly changed genes in CST cKO/KO brain showed the top targets including interferon regulatory factor 8, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), SPI1, and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein beta (C/EBPbeta), and all of them have been reported to be involved in the activation of microglia or astrocytes. We confirmed that PU1/SPI1 and STAT3 were dramatically upregulated at the protein or phosphorylation levels. Meanwhile, interferon regulatory factor 8 and C/EBPβ were slightly upregulated. Strikingly, SPI1 is one of AD risk and microglia-enriched genes (Tansey et al., 2018), and C/EBPβ has been reported to play a role in neuroinflammation and is the mediator of ApoE4 expression in AD. Furthermore, the depletion of microglia in the brain of CST KO mice demonstrated that CNS sulfatide deficiency-induced astrogliosis was independent of microgliosis. The high STAT3 levels in CST KO brain after microglia depletion suggested the STAT3 upregulation was independent of microglia and might mainly come from activated astrocytes. Thus, our new study (Qiu et al., 2021) confirmed that adult-onset CNS myelin sulfatide deficiency is sufficient to cause AD-like neuroinflammation. To further understand the association between brain sulfatide loss and glia activation, we confirmed that CNS myelin sulfatide deficiency leads to activation of microglia/astrocytes within myelin-enriched brain regions, and the activated astrocytes were adjacent to myelin-rich regions as shown via immuno staining and electron microscopy. Sulfatide has been reported to interact directly with microglia enriched membrane protein TREM2, which can promote microglial activation in response to insults to the white matter (Poliani et al., 2015); and sulfatide can also interact directly with extracellular matrix proteins like laminin (Baron et al., 2014) and tenascin (Shao et al., 2007). So we hypothesized that sulfatide deficiency-induced microglia and/or astrocyte activation begins from the loss of interaction between myelin sulfatide and ligands on microglia or astrocyte processes. ApoE ε4 allele is known as the strongest genetic risk factor for AD, and ApoE plays important roles that range from promoting amyloid-β pathology to inducing tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption. Our group also confirmed that ApoE is necessary to bring down brain sulfatide levels, as ApoE transports brain sulfatide and modulates its turnover (Han et al., 2003). In this study (Qiu et al., 2021), we found that ApoE was upregulated in the CNS of CST cKO and KO mice, which suggested myelin sulfatide deficiency and ApoE upregulation formed a positive feedback loop. However, using ApoE and CST double KO mice, we confirmed that ApoE was not necessary for sulfatide deficiency-incluced neuroinflammation, which suggested that although ApoE drives sulfatide losses in AD, it is not required for activation of disease-associated microglia and astrocytes directly. The depletion of microglia in the brain of CST KO mice demonstrated that CNS sulfatide deficiency-induced ApoE upregulation may have been primarily driven by activated astrocytes. Our study strongly indicates that specific lipid abnormalities in the brain, such as the lack of myelin sulfatides, may also be an important driving and promoting factor of neuroinflammation and mild cognitive impairment in AD pathology (Figure 1). However, follow-up studies are needed to continue to clarify how the loss of myelin sulfatide regulates brain cell functions.Figure 1: Schematic diagram summarizing how sulfatide losses cause Alzheimer’s disease-like astrocyte (A) and microglia (B) activation through a loss of interaction and a positive feedback between sulfatide loss and astrocytic ApoE overexpression.DAA: Disease-associated astrocyte; DAM: disease-associated microglia; STAT3: signal transducer and activator of transcription 3.This work was supported by National Institute on Aging RF1 AG061872 (to XH); NIH High Priority, Short-Term Project Award R56 AG061729 (to XH); National Institute on Aging RF1 AG061729 (to XH).
